title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Virginia | Genstone
metaDescription: Genstone renovates investor properties across Virginia: Richmond rowhouses, Hampton Roads coastal homes and Roanoke hillside houses, with draws and permits.
intro:
Virginia packs three very different renovation climates into one state. In Richmond, investors work with nineteenth-century brick rows, box gutters and historic review. In Hampton Roads, Virginia Beach and Norfolk bring low ground, tidal and storm flooding, salt air and a rental market shaped by the Navy. In the Roanoke Valley, railroad-era houses sit on hillside lots with stone foundations, old oil tanks and colder winters. A contractor that treats them all the same will misprice at least two of the three.

Genstone Construction renovates properties for real estate investors, lenders, servicers and funds in Virginia's major markets. Every project starts with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, then a detailed scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule, often with more than one finish level to compare against after-repair value. A designated field manager coordinates vetted, licensed local contractors, handles permits, inspections and lien waivers, and keeps progress visible without you being on site. There is no upfront payment, draws follow completed work, and dumpster costs are already in the estimate.

sections.h2: Virginia housing from the bay to the mountains
sections.body:
Virginia's housing reflects four centuries of settlement, but investor inventory clusters in a few recognizable eras.

In Richmond and other older cities, much of the stock dates from the mid-nineteenth century through the 1930s: attached brick rowhouses in the Fan and Church Hill, frame foursquares and bungalows in streetcar suburbs, and plaster-walled homes with knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized plumbing and crawlspaces. Petersburg, Lynchburg and other older cities share many of the same traits.

Hampton Roads is younger. Norfolk has a prewar core in Ghent, Colonial Place and Park Place, but Virginia Beach, Chesapeake and much of the region grew after the Second World War, producing brick ranches, split-levels, colonials and townhouse communities. Basements are rare because of the high water table, and flood zones cover large areas. Some homes from the mid-2000s were affected by defective imported drywall.

Western Virginia, including Roanoke, Lynchburg and the valley towns, has more hillside construction, with stone or block basements, retaining walls and older heating systems that once burned coal or oil.

Across the state, lead paint is common in pre-1978 homes, asbestos appears in mid-century materials, and crawlspace moisture and termites are routine findings. Polybutylene piping and aluminum branch wiring turn up in houses from the decades when those materials were used.

Each Virginia market supports different strategies.

Richmond offers a strong resale market in historic neighborhoods like the Fan, Museum District and Church Hill, where restored homes command attention and buyers expect original character. Northside and Southside neighborhoods offer rentals and BRRRR opportunities with moderate purchase prices, and student demand near VCU supports small multifamily.

Hampton Roads is a rental market built around the military. Naval Station Norfolk, NAS Oceana, Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek–Fort Story and other installations create steady demand from service members on housing allowances. Single-family rentals in Virginia Beach and Norfolk, duplexes near the bases and flips in established ranch neighborhoods all work, but flood zone status and insurance must be part of every underwriting decision.

The Roanoke Valley offers moderate purchase prices, steady demand from health care and manufacturing employers, and a growing outdoor-recreation draw. Flips do well in Raleigh Court, Grandin Village and South Roanoke, while rentals and BRRRR projects fit older and postwar neighborhoods.

FHA 203(k) renovations make sense statewide for buyers who want to live in older homes that need work, and REO renovation remains steady for banks, servicers and Government-Sponsored Enterprises managing vacant properties in all three regions.

Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, fix-and-flip loans, lines of credit and new construction loans, which can support these strategies.

Virginia uses a single statewide building code, the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code, enforced by local building departments. Independent cities like Richmond, Norfolk, Virginia Beach and Roanoke run their own permit offices, separate from the surrounding counties, so the right office depends on whether an address sits inside a city or in a county such as Henrico, Chesterfield or Roanoke County.

Permits are generally required for structural work, additions, electrical, plumbing, mechanical systems, and roofing or window replacement beyond minor repair, with rough-in and final inspections. Many Virginia cities also have local historic districts where exterior changes visible from the street need design review, such as Richmond's Old and Historic Districts, Norfolk's Ghent and Roanoke's Old Southwest.

In Tidewater, the Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act limits disturbance near shorelines and wetlands, and floodplain rules apply in mapped flood zones, including FEMA's substantial improvement standard for larger renovations.

Contractors in Virginia must be licensed by the Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation's Board for Contractors, at a class that matches the size of the jobs they perform, and individual electricians, plumbers and HVAC technicians hold tradesman licenses. Work that disturbs paint in pre-1978 homes falls under federal lead-safe rules. Genstone coordinates licensed local contractors and handles permit applications, inspection scheduling and lien waivers on every project.

sections.h2: Weather and seasonality for Virginia rehabs
sections.body:
Virginia's weather changes significantly from the coast to the mountains, and rehab schedules should change with it.

In Hampton Roads, coastal storms are the main concern. Hurricane season brings tropical systems from summer into fall, and nor'easters in the colder months push wind, rain and tidal flooding into low-lying neighborhoods. Exterior work should be dried in before storm periods, and salt air near the water shortens the life of HVAC coils and exterior metals.

In Richmond and the Piedmont, long, humid summers stress crawlspaces, attics and air conditioning. Winters bring real freezes and occasional ice storms, and summer thunderstorms test roofs and gutters. Spring and fall are the best seasons for exterior painting and masonry.

In the Roanoke Valley and western Virginia, winters are colder, with more snow and regular freeze-thaw cycles that work on masonry, retaining walls and concrete. Heating systems need to be reliable before winter, and masonry work is best scheduled from spring through early fall. Heavy rain can push water toward basements on sloped lots.

Across the state, humidity makes moisture control in crawlspaces and basements a constant scope item, and vacant properties need winterization before cold weather to prevent split pipes and water damage.

faqs.q: Which Virginia cities does Genstone serve?
faqs.a: Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed local contractors in Richmond, Virginia Beach, Norfolk and Roanoke, along with nearby areas such as Henrico, Chesterfield, Chesapeake, Portsmouth, Salem and Vinton. Projects are managed from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters with a designated field manager assigned to each job. Each market page explains the local housing stock, permits and conditions that shape renovation there, from Richmond box gutters to Norfolk tidal flooding.

faqs.q: Do Virginia's independent cities affect permitting?
faqs.a: Yes. Richmond, Norfolk, Virginia Beach and Roanoke are independent cities, not part of any county, and each runs its own permit office. A property just over the line in Henrico, Chesterfield or Roanoke County goes through that county instead. All of them enforce the statewide building code, but review timing, historic districts and local requirements differ, so we confirm jurisdiction before scoping any project.

faqs.q: Are FHA 203(k) renovations common in Virginia?
faqs.a: They are a good fit in many Virginia markets, because older homes in Richmond, Norfolk and Roanoke often need significant work, and buyers can finance repairs with the purchase. Genstone is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor and works with buyers, agents, lenders and HUD consultants on both Limited loans, up to $75,000 in non-structural repairs, and Standard loans, which allow structural work with a $5,000 minimum.

faqs.q: How does Genstone get paid on Virginia projects?
faqs.a: There is no upfront payment. Each project has a draw schedule tied to completed work, documented with photos and inspection results, and final payment comes after completion and your approval. Hauling and dumpster charges are built into the estimate rather than billed later. Completed work is backed by a one-year workmanship warranty; damage caused by tenants and ordinary wear fall outside it. Lenders and servicers who fund draws directly receive the same milestone documentation.
